objectives: Diagnose + manage common respiratory illnesses including asthma + cystic fibrosis.
Manage GI + nutritional disorders from gastroenteritis to failure to thrive.
Recognize + treat common pediatric infectious diseases.

slides.title: Respiratory illnesses: cold to cystic fibrosis
slides.body:
**Upper respiratory infection (URI / common cold)**: rhinovirus dominant, also coronavirus, adenovirus, parainfluenza, RSV, influenza. Self-limited 7-10 d. No antibiotic role. Symptomatic care only; **avoid OTC cold meds < 6 yr** (FDA 2008).

**Bronchiolitis (RSV-dominant, also rhino, hMPV, parainfluenza)**: < 2 yr, peak 3-6 mo. Wheeze + tachypnea + retractions + hypoxia. **AAP 2014/2018 guideline**: supportive care only — fluids, oxygen if SpO₂ < 90%, suctioning. **No** routine bronchodilators, steroids, antibiotics, chest x-ray, or viral testing. **Nirsevimab (Beyfortus, 2023)** — long-acting monoclonal antibody to RSV F protein — given to all infants < 8 mo entering their first RSV season. Trials (MELODY, HARMONIE) show ~75-83% reduction in medically attended LRTI. **Maternal RSV vaccine (Pfizer Abrysvo)** in pregnancy provides passive immunity to newborns. RSV prevention is a 2023-25 game-changer.

**Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis)**: parainfluenza type 1 most common; 6 mo - 6 yr; barking cough + inspiratory stridor + hoarseness, worse at night. **Westley croup score** grades severity. Treatment: **dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg** PO once (any severity). Moderate-severe: **nebulized epinephrine** with 3-4 h observation. Spasmodic croup recurs. Steeple sign on neck x-ray (rare to need).

**Pneumonia**: bacterial (Strep pneumoniae most common; Mycoplasma in school-age; Staph + H influenzae) vs viral (RSV, influenza, hMPV, adenovirus, SARS-CoV-2). Age-stratified empiric therapy: **amoxicillin** first-line for outpatient bacterial CAP in children. Vaccines (PCV13/15/20, Hib) reduced incidence dramatically.

**Asthma — GINA (Global Initiative for Asthma) 2024**:
- Chronic airway inflammation + reversible obstruction + airway hyperresponsiveness.
- ~6 million US children affected.
- **Diagnosis** ≥ 6 yr: spirometry showing reversible obstruction (FEV1 increase ≥ 12% post-bronchodilator); < 6 yr clinical + treatment response.
- **Stepwise GINA management** (Tracks 1 + 2): low-dose ICS (Track 1: ICS-formoterol as needed + reliever; Track 2: ICS + SABA reliever). Step up if uncontrolled.
- **Biologics for severe asthma**: omalizumab (anti-IgE), mepolizumab/reslizumab (anti-IL-5), benralizumab, dupilumab (anti-IL-4Rα), tezepelumab (anti-TSLP).
- **Status asthmaticus**: severe acute exacerbation refractory to bronchodilators. IV magnesium, continuous albuterol, systemic steroids, heliox, NIV, intubation if exhausted/CO₂ retention. Mortality declined dramatically since 1990s with ICS but still ~6 deaths/yr US pediatric.

**Cystic fibrosis (CF)**: autosomal recessive, **CFTR gene** chromosome 7. F508del most common mutation (~70%).
- Pathophys: defective CFTR → thick mucus → bronchiectasis + pancreatic insufficiency + male infertility (CBAVD) + meconium ileus + sinusitis.
- **Diagnosis**: newborn screening (IRT then DNA, universal in US since ~2010); **sweat chloride test** ≥ 60 mmol/L confirms (Gibson + Cooke 1959 method).
- **CFTR modulators** transformed CF since 2012: ivacaftor (Kalydeco — gating mutations), lumacaftor/ivacaftor (Orkambi), tezacaftor/ivacaftor (Symdeko), **elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (Trikafta, 2019)** for F508del — ~90% of CF patients. Life expectancy projected to rise from ~30 yr (1990) to 60+ yr.
- Adjuncts: airway clearance, dornase alfa, hypertonic saline, inhaled antibiotics (tobramycin for Pseudomonas), pancreatic enzyme replacement, fat-soluble vitamins, CF-related diabetes management.

slides.title: GI + nutrition: gastroenteritis, breastfeeding, anemia, FTT, constipation
slides.body:
**Acute gastroenteritis (AGE)**: rotavirus (declining post-vaccine), norovirus (now dominant globally), adenovirus, sapovirus, bacterial (Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, E. coli including EHEC O157:H7), parasitic (Giardia, Cryptosporidium).
- Clinical assessment: dehydration severity (CDC categories: minimal < 3%, mild-moderate 3-9%, severe ≥ 9%); skin turgor, mucous membranes, capillary refill, weight change.
- **Oral rehydration solution (ORS)** — Mahalanabis + Cash 1971 demonstration in cholera, glucose-coupled Na⁺ transport survives mucosal damage. 50-100 mL/kg over 4 h for mild-moderate. WHO ORS or commercial Pedialyte. *Lancet* called ORS 'potentially the most important medical advance of the 20th century' — > 50M deaths prevented.
- Ondansetron PO for vomiting reduces IV need.
- IV fluids for severe dehydration or failure of ORS.
- Antibiotics rarely needed (consider for bloody Shigella, Salmonella in infants/immunocompromised, severe traveler's diarrhea). **Avoid antibiotics in EHEC** — risk of HUS.
- Continue feeding ASAP (BRAT diet outdated; resume regular diet).

**Breastfeeding**:
- AAP + WHO recommend exclusive breastfeeding ~6 mo, continued ≥ 1-2 yr.
- Benefits: lower infection (otitis, GE, LRI, NEC in preterm), lower obesity, lower SIDS, possibly improved cognition, maternal benefits (postpartum weight, breast/ovarian cancer reduction).
- **LATCH score** (Latch, Audible swallow, Type of nipple, Comfort, Hold) — bedside breastfeeding assessment, 0-10.
- Common issues: latch problems, sore nipples, low milk supply, mastitis, jaundice. IBCLC support critical.
- Contraindications: HIV (in resource-rich settings), galactosemia, certain medications, active TB/HSV on breast.

**Formula**: cow-milk-based standard; hydrolyzed (extensively hydrolyzed or amino-acid) for milk-protein allergy; soy second-line. AAP advises against rice cereal/honey/cow milk < 12 mo (botulism, anemia, allergy concerns).

**Iron-deficiency anemia (IDA)**: peaks 9-18 mo (transition off iron-fortified to cow milk + low-iron solids). Screen Hgb at 12 mo (USPSTF, AAP). Hgb < 11 g/dL = anemia; MCV low, RDW high, ferritin low (best test if no inflammation). Risk factors: prolonged cow milk > 24 oz/d, low-iron diet, preterm, exclusive breastfeeding > 6 mo without iron supplementation. Treatment: oral elemental iron 3-6 mg/kg/d for 3 mo + dietary modification. Untreated IDA → cognitive + behavioral effects (Lozoff cohorts).

**Failure to thrive (FTT)**: see growth lesson; weight crossing two major percentiles or weight-for-age Z < −2. Multidisciplinary evaluation (medical, nutrition, social work, SLP for feeding).

**Functional constipation**: Rome IV criteria; very common (~30% of pediatric GI visits). Most often functional (poor diet, withholding, toilet training); 'red flags' for organic disease — delayed meconium (Hirschsprung), abdominal distension, failure to thrive, blood per rectum, abnormal exam. Treatment: disimpaction (PEG 3350), maintenance (PEG 3350 or lactulose), high-fiber diet + adequate fluids, scheduled toileting, address behavioral component. Polyethylene glycol (PEG) is first-line per ESPGHAN + NASPGHAN.

slides.title: Common pediatric infections: AOM to Kawasaki to Lyme
slides.body:
**Acute otitis media (AOM)**: most common bacterial pediatric infection. Strep pneumoniae, H. influenzae nontypeable, Moraxella catarrhalis. Peak 6-24 mo.
- Diagnosis: bulging tympanic membrane (most specific), middle-ear effusion (otoscopy + pneumatic), acute onset, signs of inflammation. Otalgia, fever.
- **AAP 2013 guideline**: observation option (no antibiotic) for non-severe AOM in selected children with good follow-up; otherwise **amoxicillin 80-90 mg/kg/d** × 10 d if < 2 yr, 5-7 d if older.
- Recurrent AOM (3+ in 6 mo or 4+ in 1 yr) → consider tympanostomy tubes.
- PCV13/PCV15/PCV20 reduced AOM ~10-30%.

**Group A streptococcal pharyngitis**:
- Most pharyngitis is viral. GAS uncommon < 3 yr.
- **Centor + McIsaac criteria** modified for age; rapid antigen detection test (sensitivity ~85%) + culture if RADT negative (per AAP/IDSA).
- Treatment: penicillin or amoxicillin 10 d (or first-gen cephalosporin if allergy).
- Complications: peritonsillar/retropharyngeal abscess, rheumatic fever, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, scarlet fever (sandpaper rash + strawberry tongue + circumoral pallor), PANDAS controversy.
- **Scarlet fever**: GAS toxin-mediated rash + fever + sore throat + 'sandpaper' rash + strawberry tongue. Treat as GAS pharyngitis.

**Kawasaki disease**:
- Acute medium-vessel vasculitis, peak 6 mo - 5 yr, Asian ancestry higher risk. Most common acquired pediatric heart disease in developed world.
- **Diagnostic criteria**: fever ≥ 5 d + ≥ 4 of: bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, oral mucous changes (red lips, strawberry tongue), polymorphous rash, extremity changes (erythema, edema, desquamation), cervical lymphadenopathy ≥ 1.5 cm. Incomplete forms common.
- Untreated → coronary artery aneurysm in ~25% (predicted by Z-score on echo).
- Treatment: **IVIG 2 g/kg + aspirin** within 10 d of onset reduces aneurysm risk to ~5%. Steroids + infliximab for refractory.
- **MIS-C** (multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children) — post-COVID Kawasaki-like illness, 2020+; similar management with IVIG ± steroids.

**Impetigo**: S. aureus + GAS. Honey-crusted (non-bullous) or bullous lesions. Topical mupirocin or retapamulin for limited; oral cephalexin/dicloxacillin for extensive.

**Hand-foot-mouth disease**: Coxsackie A16 (classic) + EV-71 (severe, Asian outbreaks); painful oral ulcers + vesicles on hands/feet/buttocks. Self-limited 7-10 d. Supportive.

**Erythema infectiosum (fifth disease)**: parvovirus B19. 'Slapped cheek' rash + lacy reticular trunk rash. Self-limited; complications: aplastic crisis in hemoglobinopathy, hydrops fetalis in pregnancy.

**Chickenpox (varicella zoster)**: highly contagious; pruritic vesicular rash, fever, malaise. Pre-vaccine ~4M cases/yr US; post-vaccine 1995 + 2nd dose 2006, > 90% reduction. Acyclovir for adolescents, immunocompromised, secondary cases in household.

**Roseola (HHV-6/7)**: 6 mo - 2 yr; 3-4 d high fever then defervescence followed by maculopapular rash. Self-limited.

**Lyme disease**: *Borrelia burgdorferi*, *Ixodes scapularis* tick (US northeast + upper midwest). **Early localized**: erythema migrans bullseye rash ≥ 5 cm, expanding ≥ 1 d post-bite. Treat: **doxycycline** (now used in all ages including < 8 yr per AAP 2019), or amoxicillin or cefuroxime. **Early disseminated**: multiple EM, cranial neuropathy (CN VII palsy), carditis, meningitis. **Late**: Lyme arthritis. PTLDS (post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome) — controversial; antibiotic re-treatment not effective.

question.question: A 6-month-old presents with 2 days of cough, wheezing, tachypnea (RR 60), retractions, SpO₂ 91% room air in November. Walk through the diagnosis + AAP-aligned management.

acceptedAnswers: bronchiolitis, RSV most likely (also rhino, hMPV, parainfluenza)

steps.reveal: Bronchiolitis: lower-airway viral infection in < 2 yr, peak 3-6 mo, autumn-winter seasonal. RSV is the classic cause (~70%); rhinovirus, hMPV, parainfluenza also. Diagnosis is clinical — cough + wheeze + tachypnea + retractions + sometimes hypoxia. Viral PCR doesn't change management.

steps.prompt: Per AAP 2014/2018, what investigations are routine?

acceptedAnswers: none routinely — no CXR, no viral testing, no labs

steps.reveal: AAP recommends **against** routine: chest x-ray, viral testing, blood gases, CBC, antibiotics. CXR only if focal findings or concern for pneumonia/foreign body/atypical course. Viral testing doesn't change management. Bronchodilator trial discouraged.

acceptedAnswers: supportive: hydration, suctioning, oxygen if SpO₂ < 90%; no bronchodilators, steroids, or antibiotics routinely

steps.reveal: Supportive care only: hydration (PO or IV as tolerated), nasal suctioning before feeds + sleep, supplemental O₂ if SpO₂ < 90%. AAP recommends **against** routine albuterol, epinephrine, corticosteroids, antibiotics, hypertonic saline. High-flow nasal cannula reduces intubation in those needing escalation. Admit for hypoxia, dehydration, respiratory failure, or apnea (especially preterm < 6 wk corrected).

steps.prompt: How could this have been prevented?

acceptedAnswers: nirsevimab (2023) — monoclonal antibody to all infants < 8 mo entering first RSV season; or maternal Abrysvo vaccine

steps.reveal: **Nirsevimab (Beyfortus, 2023)** — long-acting monoclonal antibody to RSV F-protein — single dose to all infants entering their first RSV season provides ~75-83% reduction in medically-attended LRTI (MELODY, HARMONIE trials). **Maternal RSV vaccine (Pfizer Abrysvo)** in 3rd trimester provides passive immunity. Palivizumab still used for high-risk preterm/heart-lung disease where nirsevimab unavailable. The 2023-25 era is a game-changer for RSV epidemiology.

question.question: What confirms the diagnosis of cystic fibrosis after a positive newborn screen?
options: **Sweat chloride test** (Gibson + Cooke 1959 method) — pilocarpine iontophoresis stimulates sweat, chloride concentration measured. Sweat Cl⁻ ≥ 60 mmol/L diagnostic, 30-59 intermediate (further evaluation, often genetics), < 30 unlikely. Confirms defective CFTR chloride channel. Used together with two pathogenic CFTR mutations on extended panel. CFTR modulators (Trikafta — elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor 2019) now treat ~90% of patients with F508del genotype + are projected to extend life expectancy from ~30 yr to 60+ yr.
question.explanation: Sweat chloride test (≥ 60 mmol/L) is the diagnostic gold standard since Gibson + Cooke 1959. Newborn screen (IRT then DNA) finds suspects; sweat chloride confirms; CFTR genotyping characterizes mutations + guides modulator therapy. Trikafta (elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor 2019) treats most F508del-carrying patients.

slides.workedSolution: Sweat chloride ≥ 60 mmol/L confirms CF (Gibson + Cooke 1959). Newborn screen identifies suspects; sweat chloride confirms; CFTR genotyping guides therapy. Trikafta now treats ~90% of patients.

question.question: A 3-year-old has 6 days of fever, conjunctival redness without pus, red cracked lips, polymorphous trunk rash, swollen red hands + a single 2 cm neck lymph node. Diagnose + manage.
question.modelAnswer: Apply Kawasaki disease criteria: fever ≥ 5 days + ≥ 4 of (bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, oral changes, rash, extremity changes, cervical LAD ≥ 1.5 cm). This child meets criteria — diagnose Kawasaki disease. Order baseline labs (CBC, CRP, ESR, CMP, urinalysis), ECG, **echocardiogram** to assess coronary arteries (Z-scores per Boston/Dallas criteria). Treat with **IVIG 2 g/kg over 8-12 h** + **aspirin** (moderate-dose 30-50 mg/kg/d until afebrile, then low-dose 3-5 mg/kg/d × 6-8 wk for antiplatelet effect; AAP 2017 guideline supports lower initial aspirin dosing in some centers). Time-critical: treatment within 10 days of onset reduces coronary aneurysm risk from ~25% to ~5%. Repeat echo at 2 + 6 weeks. Refractory cases (persistent fever 36 h after IVIG): repeat IVIG, IV methylprednisolone, infliximab, anakinra. Differential: viral exanthem, scarlet fever, drug reaction, MIS-C (post-COVID, similar phenotype, slightly older + with GI/cardiac shock features). Long-term: low-dose aspirin if coronary involvement; cardiology follow-up.
question.rubric: Identifies Kawasaki criteria, orders echo + labs, treats with IVIG + aspirin within 10 d, mentions coronary aneurysm risk reduction, + differentiates from MIS-C.

question.question: A 12-kg toddler with mild-moderate dehydration (~6%) needs ORS. Estimate volume to give over 4 hours.
question.explanation: WHO/CDC: 50-100 mL/kg of ORS over 4 h for mild-moderate dehydration. For 12 kg: 50 × 12 = 600 mL to 100 × 12 = 1200 mL. A typical target ~60-75 mL/kg = 720-900 mL spread over 4 h, given in small frequent sips (5-10 mL every 2-5 min) to minimize vomiting. Reassess hydration + give additional 10 mL/kg ORS for each loose stool. Add ondansetron PO if vomiting prevents adequate intake. Resume regular diet ASAP (BRAT diet is outdated).

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain why ORS was called 'potentially the most important medical advance of the 20th century' (*Lancet*).
question.rubric: Mentions: (1) global child diarrhea was once a leading killer (~5M deaths/yr in 1980); (2) Mahalanabis + Cash et al. (1971 Bangladesh cholera epidemic) demonstrated glucose-coupled sodium absorption in the gut survives mucosal injury — a simple sugar+salt+water solution rehydrates effectively. (3) WHO/UNICEF adopted ORS as a global standard; can be mixed at home or as packets. (4) Estimated > 50M child deaths prevented since adoption. (5) Cheap (cents per packet), no equipment, no clinic needed, deliverable by community health workers — exemplar of low-cost high-impact health innovation. (6) Combined with rotavirus vaccine (2006+), measles vaccination, + nutritional rehabilitation, diarrhea deaths fell from > 4M (1980) to ~370,000 (2019). Concludes: ORS is the prototype of a simple, science-driven, scalable global health intervention.
